families.statement: The quantity is the exponent \(\alpha\) in \(\mathrm{bs}(f)\ge s(f)^{\alpha-o(1)}\), for a family of total Boolean functions \(f\) with \(s(f)\to\infty\). families.name: Polynomial multiplication over F2
families.statement: The input is two polynomials over \(\mathbb{F}_2\), each given as its \(n\) coefficient bits. The output is the \(2n-1\) coefficient bits of their product in \(\mathbb{F}_2[x]\). Coefficients add without carries, so this is a different problem from integer multiplication. The machine is a deterministic Turing machine with a fixed number of tapes and a fixed alphabet. Its running time counts every step, including reading the input and writing the output. The quantity is \(\kappa\) in a worst-case running time of \(O(n\log^{1-\kappa}n)\). A higher \(\kappa\) is better. The classic baseline is above \(O(n\log n)\), so it has no \(\kappa\). In it, \(\log^*n\) is the number of times we take the logarithm to bring \(n\) down to at most 1. Harvey and van der Hoeven (2022) reach \(O(n\log n)\) only if an unproved hypothesis on primes in arithmetic progressions holds.

families.statement: A Boolean circuit over the full binary basis \(B_2\) has gates that each compute one of the 16 functions of two input bits, and the output of a gate can feed any number of other gates. families.name: Zeta zeros on the critical line
families.statement: The nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function \(\zeta(s)\) are its zeros \(\rho\) with \(0<\operatorname{Re}\rho<1\). The critical line is \(\operatorname{Re}s=\tfrac12\); the Riemann hypothesis says that every nontrivial zero lies on it. A zero of multiplicity \(m\) counts \(m\) times, and a simple zero is a zero of multiplicity \(1\). Let \(N(T)\) be the number of nontrivial zeros with \(0<\operatorname{Im}\rho\le T\), and let \(N_0^{s}(T)\) be the number of those that are simple and lie on the critical line. The quantity is \(\kappa^{*}=\liminf_{T\to\infty}N_0^{s}(T)/N(T)\), the share of the zeros that are simple and on the critical line, in the worst case as \(T\) grows. A result is a proof that \(\kappa^{*}\ge c\), and it must not assume an unproved hypothesis. A higher \(c\) is better. Several results below use the Montgomery–Taylor constant \(H=\tfrac32-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx0.6725007\). Under the Riemann hypothesis, larger values are known (for example \(19/27\approx0.7037\) by Bui and Heath-Brown). Such conditional bounds do not count here. For zeros on the critical line with no condition on multiplicity, the human record before 2026 was \(0.417293\) (more than five-twelfths), by the same four authors as the baseline. Anthropic's post gives that record as 41.6%.

families.name: Z is Diophantine in Q
families.statement: A polynomial \(P(q,w_1,\dots,w_k)\) with integer coefficients defines \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\) when, for every rational number \(q\), \(q\) is an integer exactly when \(P(q,w_1,\dots,w_k)=0\) for some rational numbers \(w_1,\dots,w_k\). The polynomial must be explicit: a public list of its terms, or a public program that writes them out. Results rank by degree first, lower is better; then by the number of variables, \(k+1\); then by the number of nonzero terms; then by the largest absolute coefficient. A stated upper bound, such as degree below \(2\uparrow\uparrow 7\), counts as that value. Degree 4 is the lowest possible for one defining polynomial (Brox, and the Version 6 manuscript of Glazer and others), so among quartics the number of variables decides. A family of polynomials that defines \(\mathbb Z\) only from an unknown bound \(N_0\) on, such as the Version 15 family in 222 variables or the family in 226 variables of Jose Brox, is not a row, because no explicit polynomial of it is certified; a certified member would be. Elliot Glazer expects that, with no limit on the degree, a definition with under 100 variables is within reach; the open question is then the fewest variables of a quartic. The chart plots the number of variables of the degree-4 results and of the first construction. Koenigsmann (2016) showed that \(\mathbb Q\setminus\mathbb Z\) is Diophantine in \(\mathbb Q\). Whether \(\mathbb Z\) itself is Diophantine in \(\mathbb Q\) was open, and Mazur's conjectures (1992) predicted that it is not.
